blocks.content: A God Object does not appear overnight. It starts as a normal class that gradually attracts more and more responsibilities because it is convenient to place new functionality there. Over time, that class becomes the center of the system, knowing too much, doing too much, and depending on everything around it.

This lesson focuses on prevention rather than repair. Detecting and splitting a God Object is important, but preventing one from forming in the first place is even better. Prevention is about making good architectural decisions early so that responsibilities naturally stay distributed across the system instead of accumulating in a single class.
1. Why Prevention Is Different from Detection
blocks.text: 1. Why Prevention Is Different from Detection

blocks.content: Detecting a God Object is a reactive activity. The code already exists, and the goal is to identify classes that have accumulated too many responsibilities.

Prevention is proactive. It happens during design, before the code is written. It involves deciding where responsibilities belong, how classes interact, and how new features will be added as the system grows.

Most God Objects are not created intentionally. They emerge because one class becomes the easiest place to add new functionality. Every individual change seems reasonable, but over time the same class receives more and more responsibilities until it becomes the center of the system.
The key to prevention is ensuring that every new responsibility gets its own proper home instead of automatically being added to the most convenient existing class.

blocks.content: Prevention Technique 1: Assign Data Ownership Early
blocks.text: Prevention Technique 1: Assign Data Ownership Early

blocks.content: One of the most common causes of a God Object is shared data that has no clear owner.

When data such as the current user, application configuration, or a cache can be accessed from anywhere, new features often get added to the same convenient class. Over time, that class becomes responsible for everything.
The solution is simple: Every piece of shared data should have exactly one owner.
Before writing any business logic, decide which class owns the data and is responsible for modifying it. Other classes should interact with that owner instead of accessing the data directly.
Bad Design
In this design, one class owns unrelated pieces of state. As new features are added, more methods get attached to the same class, eventually turning it into a God Object.
Better Design
Give each piece of state its own dedicated owner.
Now each class has a clear responsibility, and new features naturally go to the correct place instead of accumulating in a single central class.
Prevention Technique 2: Use a Facade, Not a God Object
blocks.text: Prevention Technique 2: Use a Facade, Not a God Object

blocks.content: Sometimes multiple subsystems need to work together to complete a task. A common mistake is putting all that logic into one large class, which eventually grows into a God Object.

The better approach is to use a Facade. A facade acts as a single entry point for clients, but it does not own the actual business logic. Instead, it forwards work to the classes responsible for each concern.
Facade vs God Object
A God Object performs the work itself. A Facade simply coordinates existing services.
The key rule is: A facade should route requests, not implement business logic.
Example
The checkout process needs pricing, inventory, and payment services. Instead of placing all that logic in one large class, a facade delegates the work to the appropriate services.
Notice that the facade owns no business rules. Pricing decisions belong to PricingEngine, inventory management belongs to InventoryService, and payment processing belongs to PaymentGateway.
As long as the facade only delegates work, it remains a simple coordinator rather than becoming a God Object.
Prevention Technique 3: Use a Mediator for Communication
blocks.text: Prevention Technique 3: Use a Mediator for Communication

blocks.content: A God Object often forms when many objects need to communicate with each other. Over time, one object starts holding references to all the others and becomes the central hub of the system.
The Mediator Pattern prevents this by introducing a dedicated object that manages communication between participants.
Example
In a chat application, users communicate through a chat room instead of directly referencing other users.
Notice that aUsernever references anotherUser. The mediator handles all communication, preventing any participant from gradually becoming a God Object.
Prevention Technique 4: Enforce Module Boundaries
Preventing God Objects is not only a class-level concern. The same problem can appear at the module or package level.
A common warning sign is a module that every other part of the system depends on. Over time, it becomes a dumping ground for unrelated functionality and turns into a system-wide God Object.
If Module A depends on Module B, Module B should not depend on Module A. Circular dependencies cause modules to accumulate each other's responsibilities and become tightly coupled.
Another common problem is a generic utils or common module. These modules often become the default home for code that does not have a clear owner.
The solution is to define clear module responsibilities and ensure that every piece of functionality has a proper home instead of collecting unrelated code in a shared location.
2. Concrete Refactoring Techniques

Once a class has already accumulated too many responsibilities, prevention advice is not enough. The following techniques are the practical tools for pulling a growing class apart before it hardens into something nobody wants to touch.
Extract Class

Extract Class is the most direct tool against a God Object. Look for a group of fields and methods inside the class that only ever talk to each other and rarely touch the rest of the class. That cluster is a hidden class waiting to be pulled out.

The mechanical steps are consistent every time. First, create the new class and give it a name that describes the cluster of behavior, not a generic name like Helper or Manager. Second, move the relevant fields into the new class. Third, move the methods that operate on those fields, adjusting them to use the new class instance instead of the fields directly. Finally, replace the original fields and methods in the old class with a reference to the new class and thin delegating calls.
Extract Interface

Extract Interface addresses a different symptom of a God Object: callers that only need a small slice of its behavior but end up depending on the entire class because that is the only thing available.

Instead of exposing the whole class, define a narrow interface that captures exactly what a given group of callers needs, then have the class implement that interface alongside any others. A reporting module might only need a ReceiptSource interface with one method, while an admin module needs a broader OrderAdministration interface. Each caller depends on the smallest interface that satisfies it, which does not immediately shrink the implementing class but stops new callers from reinforcing the assumption that everything belongs in one place.
Move Method to the Class That Actually Owns the Data
blocks.text: Move Method to the Class That Actually Owns the Data

blocks.content: A method that spends most of its logic reading fields from another object, rather than from its own object, is a sign known as feature envy. It is a strong hint that the method is living in the wrong class.

The fix is to move the method to the class whose data it depends on most heavily. If a method on OrderManager mostly reads and manipulates fields on a Cart object, that method belongs on Cart, or on a small class dedicated to cart calculations, not on the order manager.
3. Step by Step: Refactoring a God Object into Focused Classes
blocks.text: 3. Step by Step: Refactoring a God Object into Focused Classes

blocks.content: The techniques above are easier to apply with a concrete example. Consider an OrderManager class that has grown to handle charging the customer, updating inventory, sending a confirmation email, and logging, all inside a single placeOrder method. It is still small enough to read comfortably, but every new requirement, a discount rule, a new notification channel, a retry policy for payments, has nowhere to go except back into this same method, which is exactly how a God Object grows.
Step 1: Identify Responsibility Clusters

Reading through placeOrder, four distinct clusters emerge: charging the customer through the payment gateway, decrementing inventory, sending a confirmation email, and writing a log entry. Each cluster depends on a different collaborator and would change for a different reason, which is the classic sign that they should live in separate classes.
Step 2: Extract the First Class

Start with the cluster that is most self contained. The payment logic only touches the payment gateway and the order total, so it is extracted first into a PaymentProcessor class. OrderManager keeps its remaining responsibilities for now but delegates charging to the new class.

Notice that OrderManager still directly handles inventory, email, and logging at this point. Extraction is done one cluster at a time so each step stays reviewable and each intermediate version of the code still compiles and passes its tests.
Step 3: Extract the Remaining Classes and Introduce a Coordinator
blocks.text: Step 3: Extract the Remaining Classes and Introduce a Coordinator

blocks.content: The same move method and extract class steps are repeated for inventory and notification. Inventory decrementing becomes InventoryReserver, and the email plus logging pair becomes OrderNotifier, since both fire together whenever an order completes. What remains of OrderManager is renamed OrderService and shrinks down to a coordinator that simply calls the three collaborators in order.

OrderService now reads like a short summary of the checkout workflow, and each collaborator can change independently. A new tax calculation only touches PaymentProcessor, a new notification channel only touches OrderNotifier, and nobody needs to reread the whole class to make either change safely.
Step 4: Verify Behavior Did Not Change
blocks.text: Step 4: Verify Behavior Did Not Change

blocks.content: A refactor is only safe if the observable behavior of placeOrder is identical before and after. Before extracting anything, write or confirm tests that cover the existing method: a successful order, a declined payment, and an inventory update. Run those same tests after each extraction step without modifying their assertions, so a failing test points directly at the class that was just touched instead of forcing a search through the entire order flow.
4. Warning Signs a Class Is Growing Into a God Object
blocks.text: 4. Warning Signs a Class Is Growing Into a God Object

blocks.content: Most God Objects give plenty of warning before they become painful. The trouble is that each individual warning looks harmless on its own, which is why it helps to know the pattern to watch for.

["Method count climbing quickly: a class that gains several new public methods every sprint, with no corresponding removal, is absorbing responsibilities faster than it is shedding them.","Unrelated groups of methods: methods that can be sorted into two or three clusters with almost no overlap in the fields they touch are a sign the class already contains several smaller classes.","A growing and unrelated import list: when the imports at the top of a file span persistence, networking, formatting, and business rules all at once, the class is reaching into every layer of the system.","A constructor that keeps gaining parameters: each new collaborator injected into the constructor is a new responsibility the class has taken on.","A name that only fits by being vague: names like Manager, Handler, Processor, or Service without a qualifier often exist because the class does too many different things to be named precisely.","Frequent merge conflicts on the same file: if several unrelated features all require edits to the same class in the same sprint, that class has become a shared bottleneck.","Difficulty writing a focused unit test: needing to mock five or six unrelated collaborators just to test one small behavior is a sign the class is doing more than one job."]
items: Method count climbing quickly: a class that gains several new public methods every sprint, with no corresponding removal, is absorbing responsibilities faster than it is shedding them.
Unrelated groups of methods: methods that can be sorted into two or three clusters with almost no overlap in the fields they touch are a sign the class already contains several smaller classes.

A growing and unrelated import list: when the imports at the top of a file span persistence, networking, formatting, and business rules all at once, the class is reaching into every layer of the system.
A constructor that keeps gaining parameters: each new collaborator injected into the constructor is a new responsibility the class has taken on.
A name that only fits by being vague: names like Manager, Handler, Processor, or Service without a qualifier often exist because the class does too many different things to be named precisely.
Frequent merge conflicts on the same file: if several unrelated features all require edits to the same class in the same sprint, that class has become a shared bottleneck.
Difficulty writing a focused unit test: needing to mock five or six unrelated collaborators just to test one small behavior is a sign the class is doing more than one job.

blocks.content: 5. Catching It Early in Code Review
blocks.text: 5. Catching It Early in Code Review

blocks.content: Code review is one of the cheapest places to stop a God Object before it forms, because the cost of splitting a class goes up every time more code is written against its current shape. A reviewer does not need special tooling to notice a class drifting toward doing too much, just a few habits applied consistently.

["Look at the diff, not just the new lines: if a change adds a method to a class that already has thirty methods, ask out loud whether this new method belongs there or in a smaller, more specific class.","Read the import list before reading the logic: a sudden new import from an unrelated layer, such as a persistence class showing up in a class that used to only deal with formatting, is worth a comment even if the change itself works.","Ask where the data for this method comes from: if most of the new method reads fields from a different object than the one it lives on, point that out as a candidate for move method rather than approving it as is.","Push back gently on just one more method requests: it is tempting to approve a small addition to avoid slowing a teammate down, but a class that has absorbed ten just one more methods is indistinguishable from a class that was designed poorly from the start.","Track file size and method count over time: a file that doubles in size across a few months without ever being split is a signal worth raising in a retro, even if no single review comment flagged it."]
items: Look at the diff, not just the new lines: if a change adds a method to a class that already has thirty methods, ask out loud whether this new method belongs there or in a smaller, more specific class.

Read the import list before reading the logic: a sudden new import from an unrelated layer, such as a persistence class showing up in a class that used to only deal with formatting, is worth a comment even if the change itself works.

Ask where the data for this method comes from: if most of the new method reads fields from a different object than the one it lives on, point that out as a candidate for move method rather than approving it as is.

Push back gently on just one more method requests: it is tempting to approve a small addition to avoid slowing a teammate down, but a class that has absorbed ten just one more methods is indistinguishable from a class that was designed poorly from the start.
Track file size and method count over time: a file that doubles in size across a few months without ever being split is a signal worth raising in a retro, even if no single review comment flagged it.

blocks.title: Reviewer Checklist
blocks.content: Before approving a change to a large class, ask: does this new code belong here, does it read mostly from this class or from another one, and would a new reviewer be able to describe this class in one sentence after reading the diff. If the answer to the last question keeps getting harder over successive reviews, it is time to schedule a refactor rather than adding one more method, moving the conversation from an emergency rewrite months later to a small, low risk adjustment during a normal review.
6. Common Mistakes

["Turning a Facade into a God Object: A facade should only delegate work. If business rules, calculations, or complex decisions start appearing inside it, the facade is becoming a God Object.
","Bypassing the Mediator: The mediator pattern only works when participants communicate through the mediator. Allowing direct communication between participants defeats the purpose of the pattern.
","Breaking Ownership Rules: If a class owns a piece of data, all changes should go through that class. Creating shortcuts or duplicate copies leads to confusion and multiple sources of truth.
","Ignoring Module-Level Coupling: Even if individual classes are well-designed, a module can still become a system-wide God Object if every other module depends on it.
"]
items: Turning a Facade into a God Object: A facade should only delegate work. If business rules, calculations, or complex decisions start appearing inside it, the facade is becoming a God Object.
Bypassing the Mediator: The mediator pattern only works when participants communicate through the mediator. Allowing direct communication between participants defeats the purpose of the pattern.
Breaking Ownership Rules: If a class owns a piece of data, all changes should go through that class. Creating shortcuts or duplicate copies leads to confusion and multiple sources of truth.
Ignoring Module-Level Coupling: Even if individual classes are well-designed, a module can still become a system-wide God Object if every other module depends on it.

blocks.content: 7. Quick Reference

["Why God Objects Form: New features keep getting added to the same convenient class.
","Assign Ownership Early: Every piece of shared data should have one clear owner.
","Facade Pattern: One entry point that delegates work to specialized classes.
","Mediator Pattern: Participants communicate through a mediator instead of directly with each other.
","Module Boundaries: Keep dependencies flowing in one direction and avoid circular dependencies.
","Prevention vs Detection: Detection fixes an existing God Object. Prevention stops one from forming in the first place."]
items: Why God Objects Form: New features keep getting added to the same convenient class.
Assign Ownership Early: Every piece of shared data should have one clear owner.
Facade Pattern: One entry point that delegates work to specialized classes.
Mediator Pattern: Participants communicate through a mediator instead of directly with each other.
Module Boundaries: Keep dependencies flowing in one direction and avoid circular dependencies.
Prevention vs Detection: Detection fixes an existing God Object. Prevention stops one from forming in the first place.
